title: A website for a seed round
metaTitle: A website that can face a seed round
excerpt: Investors skim a public site for what you do, why now, and whether the team ships. The site should carry the deck's clarity without turning into the deck.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, an open, readable subject for an article about what a fundraising site must show at a glance.
caption: Poppies in clear light, the subject visible at once. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a fundraising site show on the first screen?
faqs.answer: Name the product and the person it is for, in a sentence a stranger can repeat. Give the title element the plain version of that fact, and let the visible heading carry the line you want remembered. A clever name with no descriptor forces every visitor, including someone doing diligence, to decode you before they can care.

faqs.question: Should you publish the pitch deck on the site?
faqs.answer: Keep the deck for a conversation, after you know who asked. The public site should carry the product, the user, why the problem matters now, and evidence that a team is shipping. Financial detail, unreleased plans, and customer names you cannot share belong in the room, not on a URL anyone can forward.

faqs.question: How do you show that the team can ship without inflating the story?
faqs.answer: Show a real surface: a screenshot of the workflow that exists, a short note on what this version does, and the names of the people who build it. One finished path is stronger than a tour of empty modules. Skip market numbers and quotes you would not defend in diligence.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A startup website for fundraising has to survive a skim: what the company is, why now, and whether the team can ship. The site is the public version of that clarity. The pitch deck can stay in the room.

Treat the URL as a confirmation, not as the performance. A person who has seen the deck should find the same company online. A person who has only the link should still be able to say what you do.

## What the skim is checking

Investors are not browsing for delight. They are checking whether the story holds up outside the meeting. The first screen names the product and the person it serves. Nearby, the page gives a reason the problem matters now. Somewhere a stranger can see that people are building the thing, not only describing it.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on visits puts a clock on that skim. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a value proposition has to be clear within about 10 seconds to earn a longer look. An investor's associate, opening the link between other tabs, will give you less poetry than a customer might. Spend the opening on the product, the user, and a way to go deeper.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for a title that describes the page, distinct from boilerplate, so the result is not a puzzle. On this site the title element can be plain: the company name and what it does. The visible heading can be the sentence you want remembered. Both should tell a stranger the same fact. A clever name with no descriptor forces every reader, including someone doing diligence, to decode you before they can judge you.

## The site and the deck have different jobs

The deck is a sequence you control, with a voice attached. The site is a set of pages a person enters at random, often on a phone, often after the meeting or instead of one. Copying every slide onto the homepage makes a long page nobody finishes. Hiding the story because it lives in the deck makes a URL that cannot be forwarded with confidence.

Decide what is public. The product, the user, the reason the timing matters, evidence that a team is shipping, and a way to request a conversation. Decide what stays in the room. Detailed numbers, a customer list you do not have permission to publish, unreleased plans, and any line you would not want quoted back to you.

Write the public version in full sentences. Fragments that worked beside a speaker often fail alone. If a line only makes sense after a verbal aside, replace it with the aside. The aside was the real sentence. The fragment was a prompt for you.

Keep the visual language close enough to the deck that memory matches, and let the page do what a slide cannot. A real screen. A short explanation under it. A link that goes somewhere true. A deck thumbnail of a product is a claim. A screenshot with a caption is evidence a stranger can inspect without you advancing the slide.

## Why now, in a paragraph someone can check

The timing belongs in a paragraph under the opening, before the portraits. Name the change that makes this company possible this year. A cost that moved. A habit that settled. A rule that arrived. A tool that did not exist three years ago. If you cannot name the change, describe what the user does today and where it breaks. That is still a reason. A line about the market shifting is a costume.

Investors who care about timing will look for that paragraph. If it lives on a page nobody opens from the homepage, it does not exist for the visit you care about. Put it where the skim already is. You can go deeper on a second page for the person who stays.

Skip a pile of tool logos as a substitute for the reason. A logo of software you use is not why the company exists now. A sentence about the workflow you replace is closer. If you have a pilot, describe the job they hired the product to do, and stop before you imply a scale the pilot does not have. A single honest deployment is a stronger signal than a wall of implied momentum.

Public projects from a studio are a useful reminder of the habit, even though they are not fundraises. Down the Cove had to move a store and stay recognizable. Thomas Bewick had to carry a heritage subject onto a site people can still read. Your page does not need to look like either. It needs the same discipline: show the thing, and say which problem the thing is holding. Atmosphere without that sentence is a trailer for a company.

## Show that someone is shipping

Shipping, on a public site, is a surface someone can open. A screenshot of the real interface. A short note on what this version does. A changelog, once people are using it. The point is evidence of making. A mood of making, with abstract gradients and no product, reads as a delay.

If a public login would be premature, show the slice that exists. One workflow, finished, beats a tour of twelve empty modules. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public examples of interfaces with a point of view. Study the specificity. Your screen should let a stranger point at a control and guess what it does. If they cannot, the screenshot is a poster, and posters do not survive diligence.

Name the people who do the work, and name the work. Two founders, one building, one in the conversations with users, is a fact someone can test. A line about a world-class team is not. Photos help when the faces are the people. Stock portraits suggest the truth was inconvenient. In a raise, that suggestion is expensive.

The stack is worth a line when an associate will ask anyway. A product in TypeScript and React, with PostgreSQL through Prisma, deployed on Vercel, is a concrete picture of how the thing is built. It is not a moat. Do not present it as one. It answers whether the team is building a modern web product, and then it should leave the page so the product can talk.

## What to leave off the public site

Leave the countdown off. A fundraising page that performs urgency looks like a landing page for a workshop. People who invest can tell a timer from a company. They came to see if the work is real, and a clock argues with that question.

Leave the adjective stack off. Innovative, seamless, next-generation, and a model mentioned only as garnish. If the product uses a model, say what a person can do because of it, and what a human still checks. If it does not, do not borrow the word for weather. Technical readers forgive plain language. They remember vagueness, because vagueness is what they have to unpack later at their own cost.

Leave off pages you cannot maintain. A blog with a single post from the month you incorporated. A careers page for roles you will not hire. A press page with no press. Empty rooms make a small company look like it is pretending to be a department. A short site that is entirely true looks like focus, which is the rarer signal.

Leave off other people's numbers unless you can point at the document. Market-size figures copied from a slide. Growth language you would soften the moment a question arrives. A useful test: if a stranger quoted the sentence in a note, would you still stand next to it. If the sentence only works inside your voiceover, keep it in the voiceover.

A short list of public facts is enough:

- Who the product is for, in one sentence.
- What they can do in the current version.
- Why that matters this year, in a paragraph.
- Who is building it.
- How to ask for a conversation.

Anything that does not serve that list can wait for the room.

## A door for the person who wants the deck

The site should tell a serious reader how to ask. A short note is enough: name, firm, and what they want to talk about. You can send the deck after you know who asked. Putting the full file on the open web feels open and is usually careless. Links get forwarded further than you planned, and a deck written for a room becomes a document without a narrator.

Say who replies. A founder, with a name. Say what happens if there is a fit. The site's job ends when the right person is in a conversation. It does not have to perform the close. A calendar link can sit beside the note if you want the path to be obvious. Label it with the length and the purpose, so nobody thinks they are booking a product demo when you are offering a partner conversation, or the reverse.

For everyone else, including future customers who find the same URL, the page still has to make sense. A site that only speaks to investors will confuse the users you need in order to have a company worth discussing. One layer of plain product explanation serves both readers. The round-specific detail can sit one click deeper, labeled, so a customer is not asked to parse a raise in order to understand the tool.

## After the round, change the front door

A fundraising page is a season. When the round is done, or when customers are real, a homepage tuned only for "why now" becomes the wrong front door for a buyer. Keep the product explanation. Retire language that only made sense while you were raising. Update the title so it describes the company a customer is joining.

Do that edit on purpose. A stale raise on the homepage confuses the sales conversation you are about to need. People will quote the page back to you. Give them a page you want quoted. The title, the first sentence, and the action should now agree with the call you are actually taking.

The site those customers need, once a handful of them exist and the calls turn into a pipeline, is a different problem from the raise. It is the subject of [a website after the first ten customers](/blog/a-website-after-the-first-ten-customers). Read that when the public page still sounds like a round and the people on the calls are asking for something a buyer can use.

If you want to see how a finished public site carries one clear idea a stranger can read, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Those projects are not pitch decks. They are surfaces with a job, which is the standard your URL has to meet on the day someone pastes it into a chat and does not stay to narrate it.
